content: In thermodynamics, a thermodynamic system, historically referred to as a working substance, is defined as the specific portion of the universe that is being studied or analyzed. This system is separated from the rest of the universe, known as the surroundings or environment, by a real or imaginary boundary. The classification of thermodynamic systems is based on the nature of this boundary and the types of exchanges that occur across it, such as the transfer of matter, energy, work, heat, or entropy. A thermodynamic system can take many forms, such as a piston, a solution in a test tube, a living organism, or even a planet. For example, in steam engines, the system often consists of water vapor, which can perform work when heat is applied. The working substance in such systems may interact with a heat reservoir (e.g., a boiler), a cold reservoir (e.g., a stream of cold water), or a piston (which the working substance can push to perform work). In 1850, the German physicist Rudolf Clausius expanded the concept of thermodynamic systems to include the surroundings and introduced the term working body to describe the system. In his manuscript On the Motive Power of Fire, Clausius described how heat (Q) could be introduced into or transmitted through a working body, such as a fluid or vapor, to produce work. This idea built upon the earlier work of Sadi Carnot, who in 1824 proposed that the working fluid could be any substance capable of expansion, such as water vapor, alcohol vapor, mercury vapor, permanent gases, or air. During the early development of engines, heat (QH) was typically supplied by a boiler, where water was boiled over a furnace, and heat (QC) was removed by a condenser, often using a stream of cold water. The output work (W) was typically the movement of a piston, which could turn a crank-arm and, in turn, drive a pulley to lift water out of flooded salt mines. Carnot defined work as weight lifted through a height. Thermodynamics operates under a system-centered view of the universe, where all quantities, such as pressure or mechanical work, refer to the system unless otherwise specified. The discipline focuses on the flow and balance of energy and matter within a thermodynamic system. Systems are classified into three types based on their interactions with the surroundings: 1. Isolated systems: These systems are completely isolated from their environment, meaning they do not exchange heat, work, or matter. An example is an insulated, rigid container, such as an insulated gas cylinder. 2. Closed systems: These systems can exchange energy (heat and work) but not matter with their surroundings. A greenhouse is an example of a closed system that exchanges heat but not work with its environment. The ability of a system to exchange heat, work, or both depends on the properties of its boundary. 3. Open systems: These systems exchange both energy (heat and work) and matter with their surroundings. A boundary that allows matter exchange is called permeable. The ocean is an example of an open system. In reality, no system can be perfectly isolated from its surroundings due to minimal interactions, such as gravitational attraction. When analyzing a system in steady-state conditions, the energy entering the system equals the energy leaving it. For instance, consider a system of hot liquid water and solid salt in a sealed, insulated test tube held in a vacuum. While the test tube loses heat slowly through black-body radiation, the heat loss is negligible during rapid processes like the dissolution of salt crystals. Thermodynamics does not measure time directly but may impose limitations on the timeframe of a process. For isolated systems, internal differences, such as pressure, temperature, and density, tend to equalize over time. When these equalizing processes are complete, the system is said to be in thermodynamic equilibrium, where its properties remain constant over time. Systems in equilibrium are simpler to analyze than those not in equilibrium. In thermodynamic processes, it is often assumed that each intermediate state is at equilibrium, simplifying the analysis. Processes that occur slowly enough to allow each intermediate step to be an equilibrium state are called reversible processes. In open systems, matter can flow in and out of the system boundaries. The first law of thermodynamics for open systems states that the increase in the internal energy of a system equals the energy added to the system by matter flowing in and by heating, minus the energy lost by matter flowing out and the work done by the system. The region of space enclosed by the boundaries of an open system is called a control volume, which may or may not correspond to physical walls. If the control volume is shaped so that all matter flow occurs perpendicular to its surface, the flow of matter into the system performs work as if it were a piston of fluid pushing mass into the system, and the system performs work on the matter flowing out as if driving a piston of fluid. Two types of work are performed in open systems: flow work (or PV work), which is performed on the fluid, and shaft work, which may be performed on a mechanical device. These types of work are expressed in thermodynamic equations. The concept of enthalpy (H) allows for the inclusion of both internal energy and PV work in the analysis of open systems. During steady-state operation of devices such as turbines, pumps, and engines, the energy balance equation can be simplified to determine the power generation or requirements of these devices in the absence of chemical reactions.
